extracted.intended_audience: IP litigators, financial damages experts, and attorneys preparing lost-profit claims in IP cases
extracted.subtask_short: lost profit damages for IP disputes
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on identifying, proving, and quantifying lost profit damages in intellectual property (particularly patent) litigation, centered on the Panduit factors and the evidence/expert analysis typically required. Covers types of lost-profit harms, evidentiary sources, and case-management considerations across litigation phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor — Demand for the patented product
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishing demand can require business documents and financial evidence showing customers wanted or bought the patented product; financial experts typically analyze sales, market share, and other demand indicators when applying this factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor — Absence of acceptable non-infringing alternatives
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A highly contested factor that can encompass both technical and economic reasoning. The page notes non-infringing alternatives may be third‑party products or even theoretical, but experts will examine whether such alternatives were actually available or acceptable to the defendant’s customers and whether technical/economic reasons prevented adoption. Analysis can involve technical expert input, market evidence, and competitive landscape review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor — Manufacturing and marketing capability to exploit the demand
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturing and marketing capability to exploit the demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires evidence that the plaintiff had the capacity and resources to produce and sell additional units (or otherwise exploit demand) such that lost profits would have been realized; documentation can include production plans, financials, and marketing capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor — Amount of profit claimant would have made absent the infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of profit that the claimant would have made absent the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the quantitative measure of lost profits and may include lost sales, price erosion, increased expenses, injury to goodwill, and potentially future lost profits. Experts compute additional profit using company financials, cost data, margins, and other accounting/forensic analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of lost profit damages to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Lost profit damages can take many forms including lost profits related to lost sales, price erosion, increased expenses, or injury to a company’s goodwill/reputation; lost profit damages may even extend into the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When quantifying damages, consider multiple harm types (sales, price effects, extra costs, reputational injury) and whether damages extend forward in time; choose appropriate methods and supporting evidence for each harm category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and centrality of financial expert witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the Panduit framework many, if not all, of the pertinent issues for establishing lost profit damages in patent infringement disputes are argued by financial expert witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses under each Panduit factor can entail extensive discussion citing business documents, financials, emails, witness testimony, interviews of company personnel, and opinions of other technical, scientific or other qualified experts. Financial experts develop and defend economic and accounting methodologies and respond to challenges from opposing experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for evidence-based, logical, well-reasoned estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Although estimation is inherent in quantifying lost profit damages, the analysis needs to be rooted in logic and be well-reasoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts accept that some estimation is unavoidable, but damages must be supported by logical analysis and evidentiary support; opinions should connect facts, documents, and methodology transparently so they withstand scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case management across litigation phases to support recoverability
rubrics_metrics.description: From document production to legal filings to depositions to expert opinion to trial – all phases of a case can be managed to support the recoverability (or lack thereof) of lost profit damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactively developing evidence (documents, witness statements, financial records), coordinating expert work, and framing issues in pleadings and discovery increases the likelihood that lost-profit claims will be provable; attorneys should plan evidentiary development with experts in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nuance that 'alternatives' can be theoretical but must be evaluated for real-world acceptability
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-infringing alternatives can, if properly supported, even be theoretical, but there may exist technical and/or economic reasons why such 'alternatives' were not implemented by the defendant in the real world and/or would not be acceptable to its customers (or at least not all of them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing or rebutting alternative-product theories, experts should evaluate both feasibility and customer acceptance, and document reasons why theoretical alternatives would or would not have displaced the patented product in the relevant period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation of methods and evidence by litigation type
rubrics_metrics.description: The remedy of lost profit damages is not unique to IP litigation; the specific methods and evidence investigated to quantify that remedy may vary by litigation type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should adapt quantification methods and evidentiary approaches to the context (IP versus other commercial disputes), recognizing that similar remedies can require different proof strategies and data sources depending on case type.
